chapter_theme: Learning (கல்வி) is the only true beauty, a medicine for delusion and the best legacy, and it outranks birth. Because life is short, one must choose what to learn, keep learned company, and prefer the books of wisdom that free one from confusion to merely worldly study.
structure_note: The chapter moves from learning's worth (131, 132, 134), to learning against birth (133, 136), to how to learn given a short life (135, 140), to the company of the learned (137 to 139). Its last quatrain ranks books of wisdom above worldly books, turning learning toward release.

131.reading: The beauty of a man's hair, of a garment's curving border, of a saffron wash, is not beauty; the beauty of learning, with the fairness of heart that lets one say 'we are good', is beauty.

positions.position: True beauty is learning held together with conduct that lets one judge fairly that one has not strayed from virtue.
positions.quote: ஒழுக்கத்தோடு கல்வியுடைமையும் பெற்றிருத்தலே அழகு என்பது கருத்து.

positions.position: Learning is true beauty because it produces the impartial quality of being good at heart.
positions.quote: நடுநிலைப் பண்பை உண்டாக்குவதால் கல்வி அழகே உண்மை அழகு

131.nuance: Mudaliar notes that some read the three adornments as a man's (hair), both sexes' (garment) and a woman's (saffron), and so take the verse to commend learning for women as well as men; he says others give the verse other meanings too.

132.reading: Learning yields fruit in this life, does not lessen when given, makes its owner shine, and does not perish while they live; in no world do we see a medicine like it for cutting away delusion.

positions.position: Learning does not perish for as long as its owner lives.
positions.quote: தாம் உளர் ஆ - தாம் உயிருள்ளவராக வாழுமளவும். கேடு இன்று - அழிதலில்லை.

positions.position: Learning makes its owner live on forever through fame and does not perish.

132.nuance: The disagreement is whether learning lasts as long as its owner or outlasts them through fame. Mudaliar notes that learning is called a medicine without delusion being called a disease, an incomplete metaphor.

133.reading: The worthy prize salt born in brackish ground above rice grown in fertile fields; so the learned, though of the lowest origin, are to be set in the highest place.
133.nuance: The image works because the place of origin is called low only by habit: salt from barren soil is worth more than grain from good soil. Mudaliar takes கடைநிலத்தோர் as those born in a low caste.

134.reading: It cannot be taken from where it is kept, it is not lost when given to a fit person, and kings angered by its eminence cannot seize it; so what a man should leave his children as their inheritance is learning and nothing else.
134.nuance: Each clause is a way ordinary wealth is lost: theft, giving, a king's anger. Both commentators read வாய்த்து ஈயின் as giving to a fit recipient; Pope reads வாய்த் தீயின் and has learning not perish by fire.

135.reading: Learning has no shore, learners have few days, and, thought over calmly, many illnesses; so the wise learn with clear discernment what is fitting, like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water.
135.nuance: The argument for selection is arithmetic: boundless material, a short life, and illnesses that shorten it further. Mudaliar names the bird as the swan and notes the belief that it can separate milk from water.

136.reading: No one despises the ferryman for being of the lowest of the old castes, but crosses the river with his help; so take what is good from a man who has learned books, whatever his birth.
136.nuance: The argument is from ordinary practice: people already accept help from the low-born when they need it, so they should accept teaching on the same terms. The verse speaks of using the learned man's help, not of honouring him.

137.reading: If the city of those who live in the wide heaven is sweeter than when people of sound and ancient learning, free of rivalry and sharp of mind, gather and laugh together, then we'll go and see it.
137.nuance: The conditional is a polite refusal: Mudaliar reads it as saying that such joy is found on earth and not in heaven, so there is no wish to go.

138.reading: Friendship with the learned is like eating sugarcane from the tip, sweeter as one goes; association with graceless, unfeeling people is like eating it from the root end, lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea.
138.nuance: The cane is the same in both cases; only the direction differs. So the verse is about how a bond develops over time, not how it begins.

139.reading: Even the unlearned, if they keep company with the learned, gain good sense day by day, as a new pot gives its water the scent of the bright, long-prized pathiri flowers placed in it.
139.nuance: Mudaliar explains the image: the new pot is the unlearned person, the flowers the learned, and the scent good sense. The water gains the fragrance without becoming flowers, so the change is real but borrowed.

140.reading: Of all the many kinds of learning, studying worldly books while leaving the books of wisdom unread amounts only to clamour; there is no one who knows how to make confusion leave by that means.
140.nuance: Mudaliar names the worldly books as logic and grammar, and takes தடுமாற்றம் as the stumbling through births; Pope takes it as the mind's confusion that treats unreal things as real. The verse does not say worldly learning is false, only that it cannot do this.

links.note: Both deny that outward beauty is worth anything without learning: the Kural compares it to a well-made clay doll, and the Naladiyar refuses it the name of beauty.
Both say learning does not perish when other possessions do. The Naladiyar spells out the ways it differs from wealth.

On Mudaliar's reading, 132 says learning lasts as long as its owner lives; 398 says learning gained in one birth protects through seven. Shanmuganar's reading, that it lasts through fame, is closer to the Kural's.
Both rank the low-born learned above the unlearned, the Kural by comparing them to the high-born unlearned and the Naladiyar with salt from brackish soil.

133 sets the low-born learned in the highest place; 142 says excellence, gentleness and good conduct belong only to the high-born, whatever wealth others gain. Read together, learning can raise one's rank but, in 142, not those qualities.
Both make learning the best thing a father gives his children: the Kural as a place at the front of the assembly, the Naladiyar as an inheritance that cannot be taken.
Both insist on learning what is to be learned. The Naladiyar adds the reason: learning is endless and life is short.

Both say the worth of what is taught does not depend on who teaches it: the Kural says to see the truth in whatever is heard from anyone, and the Naladiyar says to learn from the learned whatever their caste.
Both make the meeting of the learned a delight. The Kural describes how they part; the Naladiyar ranks their gathering above heaven.
Both say that friendship with people of character grows sweeter with time, the Kural like a book reread and the Naladiyar like cane eaten from the tip.
Both say understanding takes on the nature of one's company, the Kural with water and soil and the Naladiyar with water and flowers.
Both make the purpose of learning the perception of what is true, which leads out of rebirth on Mudaliar's reading of 140. The Naladiyar adds that worldly learning cannot do this.

new_concepts.label_source: The verse names அழகு; 131 contrasts adornment with the beauty of learning.

source_issues: 136: Mudaliar's commentary has a placeholder, '***', where a word (probably காணாய்) has been lost.
138: the Tamil text has a corrupted character in துரி஢ன் (probably தூரின்), and Shanmuganar's verse number reads 38.
139: Pope's translation is not aligned; Mudaliar's commentary starts mid-gloss at ஒழுகின், missing the first words' glosses; Shanmuganar's field ends with the Tamil text of 140.
